blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — healthcare water-system infection prevention
stem: Why do healthcare facilities use water-management programs for building water systems?

options.A: To reduce conditions that permit Legionella growth and transmission while also controlling risks from other waterborne healthcare pathogens.
options.B: To begin water-system controls after a confirmed Legionnaires' disease case rather than managing building-water risks before illness occurs.
options.C: To verify that incoming municipal water meets drinking-water standards, which makes additional management of the facility plumbing unnecessary.
options.D: To focus water-system controls on Legionella alone because interventions that suppress Legionella have the same effect on other waterborne pathogens.

rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends comprehensive water-management programs for healthcare facilities because they help reduce Legionella growth and transmission and can also help control other water-related healthcare-associated infections. CDC further recommends an all-hazards approach because an intervention that controls Legionella may not have the same effect on other pathogens. B incorrectly treats water management as a reactive program rather than a preventive control strategy. C incorrectly assumes municipal drinking-water compliance removes risks created within complex building water systems. D conflicts with CDC's explicit all-hazards approach.
educational_objective: Explain that healthcare water-management programs proactively control building-water conditions that support Legionella and other waterborne pathogens rather than relying only on municipal water quality or post-outbreak response.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Water Management in Healthcare Facilities; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: CDC page dated March 15, 2024 and live-rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: CDC Water Management in Healthcare Facilities lines 25-34: comprehensive WMPs are recommended and help reduce Legionella growth/transmission; lines 35-43: WMPs can control other water-related HAIs and should use an all-hazards approach because Legionella-specific interventions can affect other pathogens differently; line 68: an effective WMP is the primary strategy to control Legionella growth and spread.
source_claim_supported: Current CDC HTML directly supports comprehensive preventive healthcare water-management programs for Legionella and other waterborne pathogens and an all-hazards rather than Legionella-only approach.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: apply infection-prevention principles and protect clients and healthcare personnel from environmental hazards.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — the official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation; water-management claims are supported by current CDC HTML.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly states the preventive Legionella and broader waterborne-pathogen purposes of a WMP.
option_audit.B: Plausible outbreak-response framing but incorrect because CDC recommends comprehensive WMPs as an ongoing preventive strategy.
option_audit.C: Plausible municipal-water assumption but incorrect because healthcare WMPs manage risks within building water systems beyond source-water compliance.
option_audit.D: Plausible pathogen-specific strategy but incorrect because CDC explicitly recommends an all-hazards approach that considers other waterborne pathogens.

cueing_audit.answer_length: All four options use comparable explanatory structure and clinical detail; the correct answer is not made obvious by letter position or excessive length.
cueing_audit.absolute_words: No distractor is rejected solely because of an obvious always/never/only cue.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified: B is reactive-only, C substitutes municipal compliance for building management, and D conflicts with CDC's all-hazards guidance.
